awarenessExtra.title: Effects of Bullying on Students
awarenessExtra.intro: Bullying does not only hurt at the moment it happens. Students who are bullied again and again can carry these effects for a long time. Open a card to see what it can look like.
awarenessExtra.note: General educational content that supports the topic cards above. The school should review the exact wording before publication.

items.title: Low Self-Esteem
items.text: A student may start to believe the hurtful things said about them and feel that they are not good enough.

items.title: Anxiety and Fear
items.text: Feeling nervous or afraid of going to class, joining activities, or being near the person who hurts them.

items.title: Depression and Sadness
items.text: Ongoing sadness, crying, or losing interest in things that used to feel enjoyable.

items.title: Poor Academic Performance
items.text: Trouble concentrating in class or studying at home, so schoolwork and grades may go down.

items.title: Social Isolation
items.text: Being left out of groups and activities, or staying alone because it feels safer.

items.title: Loss of Confidence
items.text: Losing trust in their own ideas and abilities, and no longer joining recitations, clubs, or group work.

items.title: Difficulty Trusting Others
items.text: Finding it hard to believe that classmates or even adults will help or keep them safe.

items.title: Absenteeism
items.text: Missing school days, coming late, or looking for excuses to stay home to avoid the bullying.

items.title: Emotional Problems
items.text: Bottled-up anger, shame, or sudden mood changes that are hard for the student to explain.

items.title: Difficulty Building Relationships
items.text: Keeping distance from other people, which makes friendships harder to start or to keep.

awarenessExtra.title: Consequences for Students Who Repeatedly Bully Other Students
awarenessExtra.intro: Bullying is a choice, and choices have results. These are the consequences a student can face when hurtful behavior continues over time.
awarenessExtra.note: General educational content about school discipline and its effects. The school should review the exact wording, and use its own approved disciplinary rules, before publication.

items.title: School Disciplinary Actions
items.text: Breaking school rules against bullying can lead to warnings, parent conferences, or heavier penalties under the school's disciplinary rules.

items.title: Loss of Respect
items.text: Classmates, teachers, and family may lose respect and trust when someone keeps hurting other people.

items.title: Damaged Relationships
items.text: Friends and classmates may pull away, and friendships that mattered can end.

items.title: Negative Reputation
items.text: Being known as someone who bullies can follow a student and change how others treat them.

items.title: Difficulty Making Friends
items.text: Other students avoid getting close when they are afraid the same behavior will happen to them.

items.title: Academic Consequences
items.text: Lessons missed because of discipline cases, and a record that can affect school activities and opportunities.

items.title: Lack of Empathy
items.text: People who keep hurting others can stop noticing how other people feel, which makes it harder for them to change.

items.title: Possible Legal Consequences
items.text: Serious or repeated bullying, including online bullying, can have legal consequences under school policies and Philippine law.

pledge.title: My Digital Kindness Pledge
pledge.intro: I promise to help keep our school safe and respectful. I will:
lines: Use kind and respectful words, online and in school.
Never post, forward, or comment on content that is meant to hurt someone.
Include classmates instead of leaving them out.
Stand up safely for others, and ask a trusted adult for help.
Think before I click, post, or share.
Treat every classmate the way I want to be treated.
pledge.closing: Signed with my word of honor.

myths.myth: Bullying is just a normal part of growing up.
myths.fact: Bullying is harmful, and it is preventable.
myths.explanation: Repeated harm can affect a student's health, studies, and confidence. Schools are expected to take bullying seriously.

myths.myth: Only boys are involved in bullying, and only physical harm counts.
myths.fact: Bullying takes many forms, and anyone can be involved.
myths.explanation: Verbal, physical, cyber, social, and emotional bullying all cause real harm, and all of them can be reported.

myths.myth: If you are being bullied, you should just ignore it.
myths.fact: Telling a trusted adult is a strong, safe step.
myths.explanation: Repeated bullying rarely stops on its own. A trusted adult can help protect you and change what is happening.

myths.myth: Reporting a concern only makes things worse.
myths.fact: School procedures exist to protect students.
myths.explanation: A class adviser, the Guidance Office, or another trusted adult can act while keeping your concern as private as school policy allows.

myths.myth: People who bully are always strangers online.
myths.fact: Bullying often comes from people the learner already knows.
myths.explanation: Classmates, friends, and acquaintances can be involved, whether it happens in person or online.

myths.myth: It is not really bullying if it happens online.
myths.explanation: Hurtful messages, posts, and deliberate exclusion online cause the same kind of harm, and they can be reported.

tips: If a message makes you angry, wait before replying. You can always respond later.
If you are being bullied online, save evidence first (screenshots), then talk to a trusted adult.
Sit with someone who is eating alone. Inclusion is prevention.
Laughing along is still joining in. Practice saying nothing, or changing the subject.
Ask a classmate how they are doing. Kindness grows when it is noticed.
Check your privacy settings today. Only people you trust should see your posts.
If you are not sure whether something is bullying, ask a trusted adult.
Being kind online is the same as being kind in person.
When you see someone left out, invite them in.
Telling an adult is not snitching. It is keeping people safe.

items.a: It is repeated harmful behavior that hurts, embarrasses, or threatens someone. It can be words, actions, deliberate exclusion, or behavior online.
Not automatically. Bullying usually involves repeated behavior and a power imbalance. When you are unsure, ask a trusted adult for guidance.
Yes. Hurtful messages, embarrassing posts, group-chat exclusion, and sharing private content without permission are cyberbullying.

items.q: What are the forms of bullying?
items.a: Verbal, physical, cyber, social or relational, and psychological or emotional. The Awareness section explains each one, with examples and signs.
A class adviser, a teacher, the Guidance Office, a parent, or any trusted adult. The Report section shows the school's approved steps.

items.q: Will I get in trouble if I report?
items.a: Reporting is not a punishment. School procedures exist to protect students; the school's policy explains who handles a concern and how.

items.q: What should I bring when I report?
items.a: What happened, when and where it happened, and any evidence such as screenshots. Writing it down first can help you explain clearly.

items.q: Is the concern form on this site sent to the school?
items.a: No. It is a demonstration that shows the layout only. Please talk to a trusted adult or the Guidance Office directly.

items.q: Do I need an account to use the website?
items.a: No. The site works without a login, and your learning progress is kept only in this browser.
Select Start Learning in the banner to open the video lessons, or open the Awareness section to learn about each form of bullying.
Yes. Handbook pages, the kindness pledge, and the certificate are print-friendly. Use your browser's Print option.

items.q: Why does a lesson show no video?
items.a: Videos are added by the school. When a lesson has no approved video yet, the player says so honestly instead of pretending.
